title: HTTP fundamentals (request/response, headers, body)
hook: Every Web API call is a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) message: a client sends a request with a method, URL, headers, and optional body; the server returns a status code, headers, and optional body. ASP.NET Core maps that wire format into HttpContext.

blocks.text: HTTP is the application-layer protocol browsers and API clients use to talk to servers. A request names what you want (method + path), carries metadata (headers), and may include a payload (body). A response reports success or failure (status code), returns metadata (headers), and may include a payload. In ASP.NET Core, Kestrel parses the raw bytes into HttpRequest and HttpResponse objects exposed through HttpContext per connection.

entries.plainDefinition: A text-based request/response protocol for transferring representations of resources over a network.
Key-value metadata on a request or response — content type, authorization, caching directives, correlation IDs.
The optional payload after headers — JSON, form data, file bytes. GET requests usually have no body.
ASP.NET Core's per-request object holding Request, Response, Items, and user identity for the lifetime of one HTTP exchange.

blocks.text: You cannot design honest APIs without understanding what actually crosses the wire. Headers control caching, compression, authentication, and tracing. The body format (JSON, form-urlencoded, multipart) determines model binding. Misreading HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing, or HTTP/3 over QUIC leads to wrong assumptions about connection reuse and latency in production.

blocks.title: Interview baseline
blocks.body: Senior interviews expect you to explain request flow from socket bytes to controller action — not just attribute routing syntax. HTTP fundamentals are the vocabulary for every later topic: middleware, auth, caching, and versioning.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: One HTTP round trip through ASP.NET Core

items.title: Client opens a connection
items.body: Kestrel accepts TCP (or TLS). HTTP/2 may multiplex many requests on one connection.

items.title: Request line and headers arrive
items.body: Method, path, query string, and headers are parsed into HttpRequest.

items.title: Body is streamed (if present)
items.body: Large uploads stream through Request.Body — do not buffer entire files in memory by default.

items.title: Middleware pipeline runs
items.body: Each component can read headers, short-circuit, or pass to the next delegate.

items.title: Endpoint writes the response
items.body: Status code, response headers, and body are sent. Connection may stay open for the next request.

diagram.title: HTTP request through Kestrel
diagram.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant K as Kestrel
  participant P as Middleware pipeline
  participant E as Endpoint
  C->>K: TCP/TLS + HTTP request
  K->>P: HttpContext
  P->>E: Invoke endpoint
  E->>P: Status + headers + body
  P->>K: HttpResponse
  K->>C: HTTP response

snippet.label: Minimal API — read request parts
snippet.explanation: Headers are case-insensitive on the wire but exposed as a dictionary-like structure. Query string is separate from the path. Always propagate correlation IDs from inbound headers to logs and outbound calls.

snippet.label: POST with JSON body binding
snippet.explanation: ReadFromJsonAsync deserializes the request body stream. Content-Type: application/json is expected. CancellationToken flows from Kestrel when the client disconnects.

snippet.label: Set response headers explicitly
snippet.explanation: Response headers are set before the body is written. Cache-Control on dynamic PDFs prevents CDN misuse. Append adds a header without replacing existing values.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming GET requests never carry a body — some clients send one, but proxies may strip it. Reading Request.Body twice without enabling buffering. Forgetting Content-Type on JSON responses (Results.Json sets it automatically; manual WriteAsync does not). Logging full Authorization headers in production.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: enable Kestrel connection logging and compare HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 request counts per connection in Application Insights. Watch for 499 (client closed) spikes when mobile clients cancel in-flight calls. Use dotnet-trace with Microsoft-AspNetCore-Hosting to see time spent in header parsing vs endpoint execution. Large file uploads should use streaming — buffering a 500 MB body into a byte[] will OOM the pod.

blocks.title: HTTP version tradeoffs
rows: One request at a time per connection (pipelining rare)
Many connections behind load balancers — tune connection limits
Head-of-line blocking at TCP layer; great for browser APIs
Faster handshake on lossy networks; check firewall UDP rules
X-Forwarded-* headers must be trusted only from the proxy

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'HTTP is just JSON over TCP' — it is a structured message format with methods, status codes, and cache semantics. Claiming headers are case-sensitive on the wire. Not knowing that HttpContext is scoped per request and must not be captured in singleton services.

interviewTakeaways: HTTP is request (method, URL, headers, body) + response (status, headers, body); ASP.NET Core exposes this as HttpContext per request.
Stream large bodies; do not buffer entire uploads. GET usually has no body — do not rely on one.
Propagate X-Correlation-Id (or trace context) from inbound headers through logs and HttpClient outbound calls.

60s: Client sends HTTP request. Kestrel parses into HttpContext. Middleware pipeline runs. Endpoint sets status, headers, body. Connection may reuse for HTTP/2. Headers carry auth, caching, and tracing — not just JSON metadata.
Follow-up: where does TLS terminate in your deployment, and how do forwarded headers affect routing?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'headers are optional decoration' gets you rejected — they drive caching, auth, content negotiation, and tracing.
Capturing HttpContext in a singleton service causes cross-request data leaks.
Strong answer: 'One request, one HttpContext. Stream bodies. Set Cache-Control and correlation headers deliberately. Know HTTP/2 multiplexing vs HTTP/1.1 connection counts behind a load balancer.'
introducedIn: HTTP/1.0 (1996); ASP.NET Core unifies HttpContext since 1.0

jsTsCorrelations.note: Express middleware receives (req, res, next). ASP.NET Core uses HttpContext with a delegate pipeline — same HTTP semantics, different object model. express.json() is analogous to [FromBody] model binding.
Browser fetch and Node fetch expose Headers as a web-standard API. HttpClient in .NET mirrors this for outbound calls; inbound Kestrel uses HttpRequest.Headers with slightly different ergonomics.
